'''''Eragrostis mexicana''''', the '''Mexican lovegrass''', is an annual grass found from North America down to Argentina. Its specific epithet "''mexicana''" means "from Mexico". Its diploid number is 60.

==Taxonomy==
''Eragrostis mexicana'' was formerly four distinct ''Eragrostis'' species: ''E. mexicana'', ''E. neomexicana'', ''E. orcuttiana'', and ''E. virescens''. They are now united into ''E. mexicana'', with the first two species forming ''E. mexicana'' subsp. ''mexicana'' and the last two forming ''E. mexicana'' subsp. ''virescens''. All four former species are related by their diploid number of 60, their flowers with three stamens, and dark brown, reticulate [[caryopsis|caryopses]]. The two subspecies differ in the occurrence of glandular depressions below culm nodes, spikelet color, and plant size. Subspecies ''mexicana'' consists of smaller ({{convert|15-50|cm|abbr=on}} tall) grasses lacking glands with more purplish spikelets, while subspecies ''virescens'' consists of larger ({{convert|75-120|cm|abbr=on}} tall) grasses possessing glands with grey-green spikelets. The former grows in compact soil while the latter grows in cultivated areas.<ref name=Taxo>{{cite journal |pages= 377–379 |title= Eragrostis mexicana, E. neomexicana, E. orcuttiana, and E. virescens: the resolution of a taxonomic problem |last1= Koch |first1= S.D. |last2= Sánchez-Vega |first2= I. |journal= Phytologia |volume= 58 |number= 6 |year= 1985|doi= 10.5962/bhl.part.14761 |doi-access= free }}</ref>

==Description==
''Eragrostis mexicana'' is a densely tufted annual growing {{convert|10-130|cm|abbr=on}} tall, with slender [[Culm (botany)|culm]]s that are either simple or loosely branching. The pale leaves are long-attenuate, growing {{convert|1-5|mm|abbr=on}} wide. The top of the leaf sheaths are bristly, with sheaths being about a half to two-thirds as long as the internodes. Its [[ligule]]s are ciliate. The ellipsoid to ovoid [[panicle]] is very lax and open, growing {{convert|4-20|cm|abbr=on}} long (usually less than half the height of the total plant), with the spreading and ascending floral branches bearing scattered [[spikelet]]s. The ovate-lanceolate spikelets are borne on ascending, stiff [[Pedicel (botany)|pedicel]]s up to {{convert|8|mm|abbr=on}} long. The straw-colored or orangish spikelets are {{convert|2-2.5|mm|abbr=on}} wide, and can be tinged with purple. The acute [[glume]]s have scabrous keels, the first being about 1.5 mm long and the second 1.8–2 mm long. The grey-green [[Lemma (botany)|lemma]]s are 1.8-2.5 mm long and also have scabrous keels.<ref name=Manual>{{cite book |title=Gray's Manual of Botany |author= Merrit Lyndon Fernald |year= 1970 |editor= R. C. Rollins |publisher= D. Van Nostrand Company |edition= Eighth (Centennial) - Illustrated|isbn= 0-442-22250-5 |page= 124}}</ref> Its hyaline [[Palea (botany)|palea]]s have scabrous keels as well, with obtuse to truncate apices. Its [[anther]]s tend to be purplish. Its [[caryopsis|caryopses]] have shallow to deep grooves.<ref name=Texas>{{cite journal |page= 897 |title= Eragrostis in Colombia |first1= Paul |last1= Peterson |first2= Diego |last2= Giraldo-Cañas |journal= Journal of the Botanical Research Institute of Texas |volume = 1 |number= 1 |url=https://www.biodiversitylibrary.org/item/107090 |publisher= Botanical Research Institute of Texas |editor= Barney Lipscomb |year=  2007}}</ref>

The grass flowers from August to October.<ref name=Manual/>

==Distribution and habitat==
''Eragrostic mexicana'' can be found in disturbed areas such as waste places and road verges, or on dry hills and mountains.<ref>{{cite book |page= 94 |title= Contributions from the United States National Herbarium |author= United States National Herbarium and United States. Division of Botany and United States National Museum |volume= 19 |series= Bulletin (United States National Museum) |url=https://books.google.com/books?id=68hLAAAAYAAJ |year= 1915 |publisher= Smithsonian Institution Press}}</ref> It grows from [[Iowa]] and [[Delaware]] down to southwest American states and [[Mexico]], advancing as far south as [[Argentina]], [[Brazil]], and [[Paraguay]], sometimes in [[lomas]] regions.<ref name=CRC/><ref name=Manual/>
